cls: Peripheral vasodilator - combined theophylline/xanthine derivative and niacin (nicotinic acid) ester
quick: Typically 500 mg orally two to three times daily with meals
Take with or after food to reduce flushing and GI upset
Caution - niacin component can affect the liver
Blood pressure, glucose, uric acid, liver function (with niacin component)
summary: Xantinol nicotinate is a peripheral and cerebral vasodilator combining a theophylline-like xanthine moiety with nicotinic acid (niacin). It has been used for peripheral and cerebrovascular circulatory disorders such as intermittent claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and chilblains. It is NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/national formulary and BNF-type sources. Like niacin, it commonly causes cutaneous flushing, and its xanthine component shares theophylline-type cautions; objective evidence of clinical benefit in peripheral vascular disease is limited.
indications: Peripheral vascular disorders (e.g., intermittent claudication, Raynaud phenomenon)
Chilblains and other peripheral circulatory disturbances

dosage.n: Taken with meals; some regimens up to 1 g per dose

admin: Take with or after food to reduce niacin-related flushing and gastric irritation
Swallow tablets whole; do not crush sustained-release forms
Flushing of the face and upper body is common, especially early in treatment, and usually lessens with continued use
Rise slowly from sitting/lying to limit dizziness from vasodilatation
moa: Xantinol nicotinate combines a xanthine (theophylline-related) component, which causes vasodilatation and improves microcirculation and tissue oxygenation, with nicotinic acid (niacin), a direct cutaneous and peripheral vasodilator that also influences lipid metabolism. Together they increase peripheral and cerebral blood flow and reduce blood viscosity/platelet aggregation, the intended basis for use in circulatory disorders.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to xantinol nicotinate, xanthines, or nicotinic acid

preg: Avoid during pregnancy as safety has not been established.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding as safety has not been established.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; limited specific data are available.
hepatic: Use with caution; the nicotinic acid component can adversely affect the liver, particularly at higher doses or with sustained-release formulations.

moderate: Statins (with niacin component, increased myopathy risk)
Antidiabetic drugs (niacin may raise blood glucose, reducing control)
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce flushing/GI effects; alcohol worsens flushing
interactions.diagnostics: May raise blood glucose and uric acid; may affect liver enzymes

monitoring: Serum uric acid in patients with gout
Liver function with prolonged or high-dose therapy
counsel: Flushing, warmth or tingling of the skin is common and usually eases with time
Take with food and avoid alcohol to reduce flushing
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness
Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, gout, ulcers, or liver problems
This medicine assists circulation but should accompany measures such as stopping smoking and exercise
pk: Vasodilatory flushing within tens of minutes; circulatory effects over the dosing period
Plasma niacin/xanthine components peak within ~1-2 hours of an oral dose
Short for the active components; requires divided daily dosing
Several hours per dose; sustained-release forms prolong effect
Store below 25-30 C, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Not FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/national formulary and BNF-type sources
Combines a theophylline-type xanthine with nicotinic acid (niacin); flushing is the hallmark side effect
Objective evidence of benefit in peripheral arterial disease is limited - lifestyle measures and proven therapies remain primary
Niacin component warrants caution in diabetes, gout, peptic ulcer and liver disease
Take with food and avoid alcohol to minimize flushing
missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as remembered, unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Overdose may cause intense flushing, marked hypotension, dizziness, tachycardia and gastrointestinal upset; xanthine excess can additionally cause agitation, tremor or arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with positioning, fluids for hypotension, and monitoring of cardiac rhythm and glucose.
